user_input: How does Bakunin's characterization of state authority in Statism and Anarchy contrast with Marx's view on the transitional function of the state in Critique of the Gotha Programme?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy> That is because no state, not even the most republican and democratic, not even the pseudo-popular state contemplated by Marx, in essence represents anything but government of the masses from above downward, by an educated and thereby privileged minority which supposedly understands the real interests of the people better than the people themselves.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme> Now, since the state is merely a transitional institution of which use is made in the struggle, in the revolution, to keep down one’s enemies by force, it is utter nonsense to speak of a free people’s state; so long as the proletariat still makes use of the state, it makes use of it, not for the purpose of freedom, but of keeping down its enemies and, as soon as there can be any question of freedom, the state as such ceases to exist.
reference: Bakunin argues in Statism and Anarchy that all states, even democratic ones or Marx's proposed popular state, inherently represent elite governance from above downward by a privileged minority. In contrast, Marx (in Critique of the Gotha Programme, as articulated by Engels) defines the state as a temporary, transitional instrument used during revolution solely to suppress political enemies by force. While Bakunin views state power as inherently oppressive and anti-popular, Marx contends that the state is utilized for forcible repression during revolutionary struggle, and that the state as such ceases to exist once true freedom becomes possible.

user_input: In what ways does John Stuart Mill's harm principle in On Liberty diverge from Mikhail Bakunin's concept of individual freedom in the Revolutionary Catechism?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> That principle is, that the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Revolutionary Catechism> It is not true that the freedom of one man is limited by that of other men. Man is really free to the extent that his freedom, fully acknowledged and mirrored by the free consent of his fellowmen, finds confirmation and expansion in their liberty. Man is truly free only among equally free men; the slavery of even one human being violates humanity and negates the freedom of all.
reference: Mill's harm principle in On Liberty asserts that society is only warranted in interfering with an individual's liberty to prevent harm to others, holding that a person's own physical or moral good is never a sufficient reason for coercion. Conversely, Bakunin rejects the notion in the Revolutionary Catechism that individual freedom is limited or bounded by the freedom of others, maintaining instead that freedom expands through the liberty of fellow human beings. While Mill establishes a negative boundary based on self-protection against external interference, Bakunin frames freedom as an interdependent social condition requiring absolute equality and mutual recognition.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's account of women's moral education in The Subjection of Women compare with Karl Marx's analysis of female industrial labor in Capital, Volume 1?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women> All women are brought up from the very earliest years in the belief that their ideal of character is the very opposite to that of men; not self-will, and government by self-control, but submission, and yielding to the control of others. All the moralities tell them that it is the duty of women, and all the current sentimentalities that it is their nature, to live for others; to make complete abnegation of themselves, and to have no life but in their affections.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 1> However terrible and disgusting the dissolution, under the capitalist system, of the old family ties may appear, nevertheless, modern industry, by assigning as it does an important part in the process of production, outside the domestic sphere, to women, to young persons, and to children of both sexes, creates a new economic foundation for a higher form of the family and of the relations between the sexes.
reference: In The Subjection of Women, Mill focuses on moral and cultural conditioning, asserting that women are systematically educated from childhood to embrace submission, self-sacrifice, and yielding to male control as their natural duty. In contrast, Marx argues in Capital, Volume 1 that capitalist industrial production transforms gender relations by assigning women and children economic roles outside the domestic sphere. While Mill analyzes the perpetuation of subjection through ideological and educational norms within the traditional family, Marx identifies industrial labor as dissolving old family ties while creating a new economic foundation for higher forms of relations between the sexes.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's description of the structural organisation of the Paris Commune in The Civil War in France contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's revolutionary stance in Letters to a Frenchman on the Present Crisis?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, The Civil War in France> The Commune was formed of the municipal councillors, chosen by universal suffrage in the various wards of the town, responsible and revocable at short terms. The majority of its members were naturally working men, or acknowledged representatives of the working class. The Commune was to be a working, not a parliamentary body, executive and legislative at the same time.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Letters to a Frenchman on the Present Crisis> The means and condition if not the principal aim of the revolution is the annihilation of the principle of authority in all its possible manifestations, it is the complete abolition of the political and legal State, because the State, younger brother of the Church is, as Proudhon has well demonstrate, the historical consecration of all the despotisms and all the privileges, the political reasons of all the economic and social enslavements, the very essence and the center of all reaction.
reference: In The Civil War in France, Marx praises the Paris Commune as a functional working body that combined executive and legislative functions, composed of municipal councillors chosen by universal suffrage who were accountable and revocable at short terms. On the other hand, Bakunin insists in Letters to a Frenchman on the Present Crisis that a true revolution requires the complete destruction and abolition of the political and legal state and the principle of authority altogether. While Marx endorses the Commune's new institutional form of working-class governance, Bakunin maintains that establishing any state apparatus—even a provisional one—serves as the center of reaction rather than freedom.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's justification for extending suffrage in Considerations on Representative Government contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's assessment of political obedience in his Letter to La Liberté?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government> It is not, however, necessary to affirm even thus much in order to support the claim of all to participate in the sovereign power. We need not suppose that when power resides in an exclusive class, that class will knowingly and deliberately sacrifice the other classes to themselves: it suffices that, in the absence of its natural defenders, the interest of the excluded is always in danger of being overlooked; and, when looked at, is seen with very different eyes from those of the persons whom it directly concerns.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Letter to La Liberté> Anyone not involved in a party which takes fiction for reality will remember that even in these countries the people obey not the laws made by themselves but the laws made in their name; and that their obedience to these laws can never be anything but obedience to the arbitrary will of some tutelary and governing minority, or, in a word, a voluntary servitude.
reference: In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill defends political inclusion by arguing that when any class is excluded from sovereign power, its specific interests are inevitably overlooked or misinterpreted by ruling groups. In contrast, Bakunin asserts in his Letter to La Liberté that representative government is a fiction, because citizens do not obey laws they created themselves, but rather laws enacted in their name by a governing minority. While Mill views enfranchisement as an essential protection against class neglect, Bakunin characterizes compliance with representative legislation as voluntary servitude to a ruling elite.

user_input: How does the strategic focus on property in Marx and Engels' Manifesto of the Communist Party differ from Mikhail Bakunin's emphasis in the Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party> The distinguishing feature of Communism is not the abolition of property generally, but the abolition of bourgeois property. But modern bourgeois private property is the final and most complete expression of the system of producing and appropriating products, that is based on class antagonisms, on the exploitation of the many by the few. In this sense, the theory of the Communists may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance> What separates property and capital from labor? What constitutes, economically and politically, the difference of the classes, what destroys equality and perpetuates inequality, the privilege of the minority and the slavery of the majority? It is the right of inheritance. As long as the right of inheritance functioned, we could not have economic, social and political equality in the world, and as long as the inequality exists, there will be oppression and exploitation.
reference: In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels summarize communist theory as the abolition of modern bourgeois private property, which they identify as the ultimate system of class exploitation and appropriation. Conversely, Bakunin argues in the Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance that the right of inheritance is the primary legal mechanism that perpetuates class divisions and separates capital from labor. While Marx and Engels prioritize directly eliminating bourgeois private property as a mode of production, Bakunin focuses on abolishing the right of inheritance as the key prerequisite for dismantling social inequality and class privileges.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's economic criticism of Lassallean wage theory in Critique of the Gotha Programme compare with Mikhail Bakunin's critique of the state's relation to inheritance in Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme> Since Lassalle's death, there has asserted itself in our party the scientific understanding that wages are not what they appear to be — namely, the value, or price, of labor — but only a masked form for the value, or price, of labor power. Thereby, the whole bourgeois conception of wages hitherto, as well as all the criticism hitherto directed against this conception, was thrown overboard once and for all.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism> The only thing we believe the State can and should do is to change the law of inheritance, gradually at first, until it is entirely abolished as soon as possible. Since the right of inheritance is a purely arbitrary creation of the State, and one of the essential conditions for the very existence of the authoritarian and divinely sanctioned State, it can and must be abolished by liberty — which again means that the State itself must accomplish its own dissolution in a society freely organized in accordance with justice.
reference: In Critique of the Gotha Programme, Marx rejects the Lassallean 'iron law of wages' by explaining that wages represent not the price of labor itself, but a masked form for the value of labor power, thereby reframing the scientific understanding of capitalist exploitation. In Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism, Bakunin focuses on the legal structure of the state, identifying the right of inheritance as an arbitrary creation of the state that perpetuates artificial class inequalities and must be abolished to dissolve state authority. While Marx's critique targets the economic misunderstanding of wage-labor value, Bakunin focuses on legislative abolition of inheritance to eliminate state-sanctioned class privilege.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's foundational criterion for morality in Utilitarianism compare with Mikhail Bakunin's definition of moral action in God and the State?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism> The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. By happiness is intended pleasure, and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain, and the privation of pleasure.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State> Liberty, morality, and the humane dignity of man consist precisely in that man does good not because he is ordered to do so, but because he conceives it, wants it, and loves it.
reference: In Utilitarianism, Mill establishes the Greatest Happiness Principle as the foundation of morals, asserting that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote aggregate pleasure and absence of pain. In contrast, Bakunin emphasizes autonomous volition in God and the State, arguing that true morality and human dignity consist in performing good actions freely because one conceives and loves them, rather than out of command or utility calculations. While Mill evaluates morality based on consequential outcomes of happiness and pain reduction, Bakunin grounds morality in voluntary internal motivation free from external authority.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's concept of individuality in On Liberty compare with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' vision of non-specialized activity in The German Ideology?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> As it is useful that while mankind are imperfect there should be different opinions, so is it that there should be different experiments of living; that free scope should be given to varieties of character, short of injury to others; and that the worth of different modes of life should be proved practically, when any one thinks fit to try them. It is desirable, in short, that in things which do not primarily concern others, individuality should assert itself.

<2-hop: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The German Ideology> For as soon as the distribution of labour comes into being, each man has a particular, exclusive sphere of activity, which is forced upon him and from which he cannot escape... while in communist society, where nobody has one exclusive sphere of activity but each can become accomplished in any branch he wishes, society regulates the general production and thus makes it possible for me to do one thing today and another tomorrow, to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic.
reference: In On Liberty, Mill advocates for individuality through 'experiments of living,' arguing that diverse modes of life and personal character should be freely pursued without hindrance so long as they do not injure others. In The German Ideology, Marx and Engels criticize the division of labor for forcing individuals into fixed, single occupations, envisioning a communist society where general regulation allows individuals to engage in various activities like hunting, fishing, or criticizing without being confined to a specific profession. Both texts champion the flourishing of human potential beyond rigid social constraints, but Mill grounds this in self-regarding individual choice, whereas Marx and Engels tie it to the communist abolition of the division of labor.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's distinction regarding property bequest in Principles of Political Economy compare with Mikhail Bakunin's stance on inheritance in On the Question of the Right of Inheritance?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Principles of Political Economy> It follows, therefore, that although the right of bequest, or gift after death, forms part of the idea of private property, the right of inheritance, as distinguished from bequest, does not. That the property of persons who have made no disposition of it during their lifetime should pass first to their children, and, failing them, to the nearest relations, may be a proper arrangement or not, but is no consequence of the principle of private property. I see no reason why collateral inheritance should exist at all.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, On the Question of the Right of Inheritance> The right of inheritance, once the natural result of the violent appropriation of natural and social riches, became the basis of the political State and the juridical family, which guarantee and sanction individual property. We must therefore vote to abolish, the right of inheritance.
reference: In Principles of Political Economy, Mill distinguishes between the right of bequest (which he includes in the idea of private property) and the right of intestate inheritance, arguing that passing property to collateral relatives is not an essential consequence of private property rights. In contrast, Bakunin takes a far more radical position in On the Question of the Right of Inheritance, demanding the total abolition of all inheritance rights because they serve as the foundational legal sanction for private property, class division, and the political state. While Mill seeks to limit unearned family transfers while preserving individual bequest, Bakunin targets the complete elimination of inheritance as a necessary step toward social liquidation.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's characterization of state security in Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism compare with John Stuart Mill's perspective on equal social relations in Utilitarianism?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism> Such are the internal conditions that necessarily result for the State from its objective stance, that is, its natural, permanent, and inevitable hostility toward all the other states... The State not only has the mission of guaranteeing the safety of its members against any attack coming from without; it must also defend them within its own borders, some of them against the others, and each of them against himself.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism> Society between human beings, except in the relation of master and slave, is manifestly impossible on any other footing than that the interests of all are to be consulted. Society between equals can only exist on the understanding that the interests of all are to be regarded equally. And since in all states of civilization, every person, except an absolute monarch, has equals, every one is obliged to live on these terms with somebody...
reference: In Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism, Bakunin describes the state as inherently hostile to other states and driven internally to police its citizens against one another and against themselves, assuming human nature to be inherently wicked. In contrast, Mill argues in Utilitarianism that genuine human society among equals can only exist on the foundation of equal consideration of all members' interests, which naturally becomes an inseparable part of civilization as social ties strengthen. While Bakunin views the state as an artificial coercive apparatus built on mutual distrust, Mill sees the growth of equal social consideration as a natural sentiment necessary for social co-existence.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's analysis of the French state bureaucracy in The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte compare with Mikhail Bakunin's critique of the state in Statism and Anarchy?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte> The executive power with its enormous bureaucratic and military organization, with its wide-ranging and ingenious state machinery, with a host of officials numbering half a million, besides an army of another half million – this terrifying parasitic body which enmeshes the body of French society and chokes all its pores sprang up in the time of the absolute monarchy, with the decay of the feudal system which it had helped to hasten.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy> If there is a state, then necessarily there is domination and consequently slavery. A state without slavery, open or camouflaged, is inconceivable – that is why we are enemies of the state. What does it mean, 'the proletariat raised to a governing class?' Will the entire proletariat head the government?
reference: In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, Marx analyzes the French executive state power as a massive bureaucratic and military parasitic body that historical development centralized and expanded to enmesh civil society. In Statism and Anarchy, Bakunin similarly characterizes the state as a dominant power soaring above society, but concludes that any state fundamentally necessitates domination and slavery, whether open or camouflaged. Both thinkers diagnose the modern centralized state machinery as a suffocating, parasitic force, though Marx analyzes its historical emergence under specific French class conditions while Bakunin treats all state existence as inherently incompatible with freedom.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's economic analysis of product exchange in Poverty of Philosophy contrast with John Stuart Mill's view of trade regulation in On Liberty?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Poverty of Philosophy> In general, the form of exchange of products corresponds to the form of production. Change the latter, and the former will change in consequence. Thus in the history of society we see that the mode of exchanging products is regulated by the mode of producing them. Individual exchange corresponds also to a definite mode of production which itself corresponds to class antagonism. There is thus no individual exchange without the antagonism of classes.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> As the principle of individual liberty is not involved in the doctrine of Free Trade, so neither is it in most of the questions which arise respecting the limits of that doctrine: as for example, what amount of public control is admissible for the prevention of fraud by adulteration; how far sanitary precautions, or arrangements to protect work-people employed in dangerous occupations, should be enforced on employers.
reference: In Poverty of Philosophy, Marx asserts that the mode of product exchange is directly determined by the mode of production and that individual commodity exchange inherently corresponds to class antagonism. In On Liberty, Mill treats trade as a social act distinct from personal liberty, maintaining that free trade and market regulation (such as sanitary rules or employer safety standards) are matters of public policy rather than individual rights. While Marx links individual market exchange directly to structural class exploitation and historical modes of production, Mill evaluates trade controls as social expediency measures that do not infringe upon core individual freedom.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's conclusion regarding wage struggles in Value, Price and Profit compare with Mikhail Bakunin's characterization of capital in The Capitalist System?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Value, Price and Profit> They ought to understand that, with all the miseries it imposes upon them, the present system simultaneously engenders the material conditions and the social forms necessary for an economical reconstruction of society. Instead of the conservative motto: 'A fair day's wage for a fair day's work!' they ought to inscribe on their banner the revolutionary watchword: 'Abolition of the wages system!'

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The Capitalist System> What is property, what is capital in their present form? For the capitalist and the property owner they mean the power and the right, guaranteed by the State, to live without working. And since neither property nor capital produces anything when not fertilized by labor — that means the power and the right to live by exploiting the work of someone else, the right to exploit the work of those who possess neither property nor capital and who thus are forced to sell their productive power to the lucky owners of both.
reference: In Value, Price and Profit, Marx argues that workers must go beyond daily wage resistance and demand the 'Abolition of the wages system!' because capitalism engenders the material conditions needed to reconstruct society. In The Capitalist System, Bakunin describes capital and property as a state-guaranteed right to live without working by exploiting those who own no property and are forced by hunger to sell their labor power. Both authors agree that capitalist property relations inherently rely on compulsory labor exploitation, with Marx urging the working class to replace the wage system entirely and Bakunin emphasizing that capital is fundamentally state-sanctioned non-productive exploitation.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's conceptualization of logical deduction in A System of Logic compare with Mikhail Bakunin's view of scientific authority in God and the State?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive> All inference is from particulars to particulars: General propositions are merely registers of such inferences already made, and short formulæ for making more: The major premiss of a syllogism, consequently, is a formula of this description: and the conclusion is not an inference drawn *from* the formula, but an inference drawn *according* to the formula: the real logical antecedent, or premisses, being the particular facts from which the general proposition was collected by induction.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State> We recognize the absolute authority of science, but we reject the infallibility and universality of the savant. In our church — if I may be permitted to use for a moment an expression which I so detest: Church and State are my two bêtes noires — in our church, as in the Protestant church, we have a chief, an invisible Christ, science; and, like the Protestants, more logical even than the Protestants, we will suffer neither pope, nor council, nor conclaves of infallible cardinals, nor bishops, nor even priests. Our Christ differs from the Protestant and Christian Christ in this — that the latter is a personal being, ours impersonal; the Christian Christ, already completed in an eternal past, presents himself as a perfect being, while the completion and perfection of our Christ, science, are ever in the future: which is equivalent to saying that they will never be realized.
reference: In A System of Logic, Mill conceptualizes general propositions not as ultimate sources of truth, but as mere registers of past inferences from particulars that serve as formulas for guiding future reasoning. Similarly, Bakunin in God and the State accepts the absolute authority of science while rejecting any infallible human savant or fixed dogmatic authority, defining science as an endlessly uncompleted, impersonal process. Both thinkers reject fixed, closed dogmas imposed from above—Mill treating general logical premises as tentative records of empirical facts, and Bakunin treating scientific truth as an open-ended process whose completion lies perpetually in the future.

user_input: How does Marx's philosophical analysis of alienated labor compare with Bakunin's account of how wage labor traps workers in poverty?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844> The devaluation of the world of men is in direct proportion to the increasing value of the world of things. Labor produces not only commodities; it produces itself and the worker as a commodity – and this at the same rate at which it produces commodities in general. This fact expresses merely that the object which labor produces – labor’s product – confronts it as something alien, as a power independent of the producer.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The Capitalist System> For since they possess no other means of existence but their own manual labor, they are driven, by the fear of seeing themselves replaced by others, to sell it at the lowest price. This tendency of the workers, or rather the necessity to which they are condemned by their own poverty, combined with the tendency of the employers to sell the products of their workers, and consequently buy their labor, at the lowest price, constantly reproduces and consolidates the poverty of the proletariat. Since he finds himself in a state of poverty, the worker is compelled to sell his labor for almost nothing, and because he sells that product for almost nothing, he sinks into ever greater poverty.
reference: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx explains the philosophical mechanics of alienation, noting that as the world of things gains value, the worker is devalued and converted into a commodity whose product confronts him as an alien power. In The Capitalist System, Bakunin describes the practical economic trap of wage labor, showing how the worker's poverty forces him to sell his labor at the lowest price, which continuously reproduces and deepens his poverty. While Marx focuses on how labor's product becomes an independent alien force dominating the worker, Bakunin emphasizes the self-perpetuating cycle of poverty and price depression that keeps wage laborers economically trapped.

user_input: In what ways does Auguste Comte's view of political expertise as recounted by John Stuart Mill contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's characterization of state science in Equal Opportunity in Education?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Auguste Comte and Positivism> As far as this doctrine only means that opinions, and their expression, should be exempt from legal restraint, either in the form of prevention or of penalty, M. Comte is a firm adherent of it: but the moral right of every human being, however ill-prepared by the necessary instruction and discipline, to erect himself into a judge of the most intricate as well as the most important questions that can occupy the human intellect, he resolutely denies. "There is no liberty of conscience," he said in an early work, "in astronomy, in physics, in chemistry, even in physiology, in the sense that every one would think it absurd not to accept in confidence the principles established in those sciences by the competent persons. If it is otherwise in politics, the reason is merely because, the old doctrines having gone by and the new ones not being yet formed, there are not properly, during the interval, any established opinions."

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Equal Opportunity in Education> Is it by some power inherent in their persons? No — it is solely through the power of the State, in whose apparatus today their offspring hold, always, every key position (and even every lower and middle range position) excepting that of soldier and worker. And in this day and age what is it that constitutes the principle underlying the power of the State? Why, it is science. Yes, science — Science of government, science of administration and financial science; the science of fleecing the flocks of the people without their bleating too loudly and, when they start to bleat, the science of urging silence, patience and obedience upon them by means of a scientifically organised force: the science of deceiving and dividing the masses of the people and keeping them allays in a salutary ignorance lest they ever become able, by helping one another and pooling their efforts, to conjure up a power capable of overturning States...
reference: According to Mill's account of Comte in Auguste Comte and Positivism, Comte denies an individual moral right to absolute liberty of conscience in complex political matters, arguing that political decisions should be deferred to trained experts just as individuals accept established principles in astronomy or physics. In contrast, Bakunin argues in Equal Opportunity in Education that state-sponsored 'science'—including the science of government and administration—is merely an instrument used by the ruling class to fleece, deceive, and subdue the ignorant masses. While Comte views scientific expertise as a necessary authority for establishing stable political consensus, Bakunin condemns governmental science as an oppressive tool for maintaining class privilege and political centralization.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's concept of commodity fetishism in Capital, Volume 1 contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's critique of social tyranny in Man, Society, and Freedom?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 1> To the latter, therefore, the relations connecting the labour of one individual with that of the rest appear, not as direct social relations between individuals at work, but as what they really are, material relations between persons and social relations between things. It is only by being exchanged that the products of labour acquire, as values, one uniform social status, distinct from their varied forms of existence as objects of utility.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Man, Society, and Freedom> The action of social tyranny is gentler, more insidious, more imperceptible, but no less powerful and pervasive than is the authority of the State. It dominates men by customs, by mores, by the mass of prejudices, by the habits of daily life, all of which combine to form what is called public opinion.
reference: In Capital, Volume 1, Marx analyzes how market relations obscure social ties, turning direct relations between working individuals into material relations between persons and social relations between things through exchange. In Man, Society, and Freedom, Bakunin describes social tyranny as an insidious, pervasive force that dominates individuals through customs, prejudices, daily habits, and public opinion rather than formal state laws. While Marx locates the obfuscation of human relations specifically in the economic mechanics of commodity exchange, Bakunin focuses on the broader socio-cultural pressure exerted by collective public opinion over individual behavior.

user_input: How do John Stuart Mill's observations on the tyranny of majority opinion in On Liberty compare with Mikhail Bakunin's description of social tyranny in Man, Society, and Freedom?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> Society can and does execute its own mandates: and if it issues wrong mandates instead of right, or any mandates at all in things with which it ought not to meddle, it practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since, though not usually upheld by such extreme penalties, it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself. Protection, therefore, against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose, by other means than civil penalties, its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them; to fetter the development, and, if possible, prevent the formation, of any individuality not in harmony with its ways, and compel all characters to fashion themselves upon the model of its own.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Man, Society, and Freedom> Social tyranny, often overwhelming and baneful, does not assume the violent imperative character of the legalized and formalized despotism which marks the authority of the State. It is not imposed in the form of laws to which every individual, on pain of judicial punishment, is forced to submit. The action of social tyranny is gentler, more insidious, more imperceptible, but no less powerful and pervasive than is the authority of the State. It dominates men by customs, by mores, by the mass of prejudices, by the habits of daily life, all of which combine to form what is called public opinion.
reference: Both Mill in On Liberty and Bakunin in Man, Society, and Freedom observe that non-legal, social pressure can be just as formidable as formal political despotism. Mill stresses that social tyranny penetrates deeply into daily life to enslave the soul and stifle individuality through prevailing feelings and opinion without needing civil penalties. Bakunin similarly describes social tyranny as gentle, insidious, and unformalized, operating through customs, prejudices, and public opinion rather than state laws or judicial punishment. Both thinkers highlight that public opinion and societal expectations exert an all-pervasive, coercive force on human behavior independent of state legislation.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's doctrine regarding capital and demand for labor in Principles of Political Economy compare with Karl Marx's critique of compensation theories in Capital, Volume 1?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Principles of Political Economy> It is intended, however, to establish the proposition that wealth paid out in wages, or advanced to producers, itself supports labor; that wealth offered directly to laborers in this way employs more labor than when merely offered in exchange for other goods, or, in other words, by a demand for commodities; that an increased demand for commodities does not involve an increased demand for labor, since this can only be created by capital.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 1> James Mill, MacCulloch, Torrens, Senior, John Stuart Mill, and a whole series besides, of bourgeois political economists, insist that all machinery that displaces workmen, simultaneously and necessarily sets free an amount of capital adequate to employ the same identical workmen... The simple fact, by no means a new one, that machinery cuts off the workmen from their means of subsistence is, therefore, in economic parlance tantamount to this, that machinery liberates means of subsistence for the workman, or converts those means into capital for his employment. The mode of expression, you see, is everything.
reference: In Principles of Political Economy, Mill argues that demand for commodities is not a demand for labor, asserting that only capital directly advanced in wages supports and employs laborers. In Capital, Volume 1, Marx explicitly attacks Mill and other economists for claiming that introducing machinery automatically 'sets free' capital to re-employ displaced workers. Marx satirizes this economic dogma, contending that machinery actually deprives workers of their means of subsistence rather than liberating capital for their benefit. While Mill sees capital as the sole protective mechanism for labor employment, Marx argues that capital transformation under mechanization actively locks up variable capital and displaces workers.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's view of revolutionary leadership in his letter to Nechayev compare with Karl Marx's view of working-class consciousness in Grundrisse?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Bakunin to Nechayev on the Role of Secret Revolutionary Societies> A revolutionary idea is revolutionary, vital, real and true only because it expresses and only as far as it represents popular instincts which are the result of history. To strive to foist on the people your own thoughts--foreign to its instinct--implies a wish to make it subservient to a new state... The organization must accept in all sincerity the idea that it is a servant and a helper, but never a commander of the people, never under any pretext its manager, not even under the pretext of the people’s welfare.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, Grundrisse> The recognition [Erkennung] of the products as its own, and the judgement that its separation from the conditions of its realization is improper – forcibly imposed – is an enormous [advance in] awareness [Bewusstsein], itself the product of the mode of production resting on capital, and as much the knell to its doom as, with the slave’s awareness that he cannot be the property of another, with his consciousness of himself as a person, the existence of slavery becomes a merely artificial, vegetative existence, and ceases to be able to prevail as the basis of production.
reference: In his letter to Nechayev, Bakunin asserts that a revolutionary organization must serve merely as a helper and staff to the people, warning that attempting to impose foreign ideas onto popular instincts turns the organization into a new commanding state power. In Grundrisse, Marx describes revolutionary progress as the working class's own developing awareness that its separation from the conditions of production is forcibly imposed, comparing this consciousness to a slave realizing he cannot be owned. Both thinkers highlight that true emancipation depends on the internal consciousness and instincts of the oppressed class rather than external imposition, though Bakunin explicitly focuses on preventing revolutionary organizers from usurping power.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's assessment of state morality in The German Crisis contrast with John Stuart Mill's concept of political voting in Considerations on Representative Government?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The German Crisis> Whosoever mentions the State, implies force, oppression, exploitation, injustice-all these brought together as a system are the main condition of present-day society. The State has never had, and never can have, a morality. Its only morality and justice is its own interest, its existence, and its omnipotence at any price; and before its interest, all interest of humanity must stand in the back-ground.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government> In any political election, even by universal suffrage (and still more obviously in the case of a restricted suffrage), the voter is under an absolute moral obligation to consider the interest of the public, not his private advantage, and give his vote, to the best of his judgment, exactly as he would be bound to do if he were the sole voter, and the election depended upon him alone.
reference: In The German Crisis, Bakunin characterizes the state as an inherently immoral system of force, oppression, and exploitation whose sole interest is its own omnipotence at the expense of humanity. In contrast, Mill asserts in Considerations on Representative Government that political voting within a representative state carries an absolute moral obligation to serve the public interest rather than personal advantage. While Mill believes state electoral mechanisms can express civic duty and public morality, Bakunin maintains that the state is fundamentally devoid of morality and exists only to subjugate human freedom.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's methodological reliance on general axioms in A System of Logic compare with Karl Marx's critique of individualist premises in A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic: Ratiocinative and Inductive, 7th Edition, Vol. I> The statement, that the uniformity of the course of nature is the ultimate major premise in all cases of induction, may be thought to require some explanation... The real proof that what is true of John, Peter, &c. is true of all mankind, can only be, that a different supposition would be inconsistent with the uniformity which we know to exist in the course of nature.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy> The solitary and isolated hunter or fisherman, who serves Adam Smith and Ricardo as a starting point, is one of the unimaginative fantasies of eighteenth-century romances a la Robinson Crusoe; and despite the assertions of social historians, these by no means signify simply a reaction against over-refinement and reversion to a misconceived natural life... The further back we trace the course of history, the more does the individual, and accordingly also the producing individual, appear to be dependent and to belong to a larger whole.
reference: In A System of Logic, Mill establishes that inductive generalizations ultimately rely on the foundational axiom of the uniformity of nature to justify moving from individual instances to universal claims about mankind. In A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, Marx rejects abstract methodological starting points—such as the isolated 'Robinson Crusoe' individual of classical economics—arguing instead that human individuals are historically dependent members of a larger social whole. While Mill builds inductive logic upon a universal natural axiom governing individual cases, Marx criticizes unhistorical assumptions about isolated individuals, insisting on historical social relations as the true starting point of analysis.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's characterization of patriotism in his Speech to a Public Assembly of Foreign Socialists compare with his distinction between popular and political patriotism as cited in Alfredo Bonanno's Anarchism and the National Liberation Struggle?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Speech of the Citizen Bakunin to a Public Assembly of Foreign Socialists> Whoever speaks of the State, speaks of fortresses—speaks of the violent separation of one portion of humanity from all the other portions, equally imprisoned in other State, they speak of the rivalry, competition and perpetual war of the States; they speak of conquest, dispossession and patriotic and glorious massacre, both within and without: legalized and regulate oppression and exploitation of the labor of the people, for the profit of a dominant minority. The passion corresponding to this double manifestation of the States is called patriotism. We want no more patriotism, because we want justice, human rights and human fraternity.

<2-hop: Alfredo Bonanno, Anarchism and the National Liberation Struggle> The State is not the Fatherland, it is the abstraction, the metaphysical, mystical, political, juridical fiction of the Fatherland. The common people of all countries deeply love their fatherland; but that is a natural, real love. The patriotism of the people is not just an idea, it is a fact; but political patriotism, love of the State, is not the faithful expression of that fact: it is an expression distorted by means of a false abstraction, always for the benefit of an exploiting minority.
reference: In his Speech to a Public Assembly of Foreign Socialists, Bakunin totally rejects patriotism as a passion corresponding to state power, conquest, and the legal exploitation of labor for a dominant minority. In the text cited by Bonanno, however, Bakunin draws a precise distinction between popular patriotism—a natural, real love of the fatherland shared by ordinary people—and political patriotism, which he defines as a distorted juridical fiction serving an exploiting elite. While both passages condemn political patriotism as a tool for minority exploitation and state domination, the excerpt in Bonanno clarifies that Bakunin acknowledged a genuine, non-statist love of one's homeland among the common people.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's critique of bourgeois capital categories in Capital, Volume 2 contrast with John Stuart Mill's formulation of wage determination in Principles of Political Economy?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 2> By this means the distinction between the variable and constant capital, which decides everything, is blotted out, hence the whole secret of the production of surplus-value and of capitalist production, the circumstances which transform certain values and the things in which they present themselves into capital, are obliterated. All constituent parts of capital are then distinguished merely by their mode of circulation (and, of course, circulation of commodities concerns itself solely with already existing given values); and the capital laid out in wages shares a peculiar mode of circulation with the part of capital laid out in raw materials, semi-finished products, auxiliary materials, as opposed to the part of capital laid out in instruments of labour.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, Principles of Political EconomyAbridged with Critical, Bibliographical, and Explanatory Notes, and a Sketch of the History of Political Economy> I believe that, in the existing state of the national wealth, the character of Englishmen being what it is, a certain prospect of profit will "determine" a certain proportion of this wealth to productive investment; that the amount thus "determine" will increase as the field for investment is extended... while this, the form of the investment, will again "determine" the proportion of the whole capital which shall be paid as wages to laborers.
reference: In Capital, Volume 2, Marx criticizes classical economists for conflating constant/variable capital with fixed/circulating capital, arguing that treating wages merely as circulating capital obliterates the secret of surplus-value production. In Principles of Political Economy (as excerpted via Cairnes's restatement), Mill treats capital and wages through investment proportions, holding that profit expectations and investment forms determine the predetermined share of capital paid out as wages to laborers. While Mill analyzes wage-fund allocation based on circulation and investment proportions, Marx insists that such circulation-focused frameworks obscure the fundamental distinction between value-creating variable capital and constant capital.

user_input: How does James Mill's explanation of moral sanction in Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind compare with Mikhail Bakunin's account of popular experience in God and the State?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind> It is from the great use made of those acts in the Education of children, and even in the rude management of them in the nursery, that praise and blame acquire the influence in most cases, the ascendancy in some, which they are seen to exercise over us. It is this sensibility to praise and blame, in other words, the associations we have with them, which gives its effect to what is called POPULAR OPINION, or the POPULAR SANCTION, and, when the acts of Justice, Beneficence, Fortitude, and Prudence of other men are the objects of it, the MORAL SANCTION; *Popular Opinion*, being a phrase which expresses the Praise or Blame which the people bestow; and the *Sanction* being the good or evil consequences which men are accustomed to associate with that praise or blame.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State> The practical summary of their painful experiences constitutes a sort of traditional science, which in certain respects is worth as much as theoretical science. Last of all, a portion of the youth — those of the bourgeois students who feel hatred enough for the falsehood, hypocrisy, injustice, and cowardice of the bourgeoisie to find courage to turn their backs upon it, and passion enough to unreservedly embrace the just and human cause of the proletariat — those will be, as I have already said, fraternal instructors of the people; thanks to them, there will be no occasion for the government of the savants.
reference: In Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind, James Mill (edited/discussed by John Stuart Mill) explains moral sanction as a psychological product of nursery education and association, where praise and blame form the basis of popular opinion and moral judgment. In God and the State, Bakunin grounds popular morality not in psychological conditioning, but in the practical, historical experience of the working people, which forms a traditional science worth as much as theoretical science. While James Mill attributes moral sanctions to acquired associations of praise and blame, Bakunin focuses on the lived historical struggles of the masses as the source of popular wisdom and emancipation.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's critique of interest-bearing capital in Capital, Volume 3 compare with Mikhail Bakunin's description of market compulsion in The Capitalist System?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 3> In M — M' we have the meaningless form of capital, the perversion and objectification of production relations in their highest degree, the interest-bearing form, the simple form of capital, in which it antecedes its own process of reproduction. It is the capacity of money, or of a commodity, to expand its own value independently of reproduction — which is a mystification of capital in its most flagrant form. For vulgar political economy, which seeks to represent capital as an independent source of value, of value creation, this form is naturally a veritable find, a form in which the source of profit is no longer discernible, and in which the result of the capitalist process of production — divorced from the process — acquires an independent existence.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The Capitalist System> For since they possess no other means of existence but their own manual labor, they are driven, by the fear of seeing themselves replaced by others, to sell it at the lowest price. This tendency of the workers, or rather the necessity to which they are condemned by their own poverty, combined with the tendency of the employers to sell the products of their workers, and consequently buy their labor, at the lowest price, constantly reproduces and consolidates the poverty of the proletariat.
reference: In Capital, Volume 3, Marx demonstrates how interest-bearing capital (M—M') creates the ultimate fetish and mystification by appearing to generate money out of money independently of production relations, thereby obscuring the true source of profit. In The Capitalist System, Bakunin reveals the real social underlying mechanism that Marx's fetishized form conceals, showing that capitalist gain relies on the economic compulsion of propertyless workers who are forced by poverty to sell their labor at minimum prices. While Marx criticizes the ideological illusion that capital generates self-expanding value on its own, Bakunin highlights the concrete social compulsion and exploitation of labor that actually sustains the capitalist system.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's formulation of agricultural rent in Principles of Political Economy compare with Karl Marx's analysis of ground-rent in Capital, Volume 3?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, Principles of Political EconomyAbridged with Critical, Bibliographical, and Explanatory Notes, and a Sketch of the History of Political Economy> Rent the Effect of a Natural Monopoly. No Land can pay Rent except Land of such Quality or Situation as exists in less Quantity than the Demand. The Rent of Land is the Excess of its Return above the Return to the worst Land in Cultivation. —Or to the Capital employed in the least advantageous Circumstances.

<2-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 3> Wage-labour and landed property, like capital, are historically determined social forms; one of labour, the other of monopolised terrestrial globe, and indeed both forms corresponding to capital and belonging to the same economic formation of society... But how should land create value, i.e., a socially defined quantity of labour, and moreover that particular portion of the value of its own products which forms the rent? Land, e.g., takes part as an agent of production in creating a use-value, a material product, wheat. But it has nothing to do with the production of the value of wheat.
reference: In Principles of Political Economy, Mill defines rent as the result of a natural monopoly, calculated as the excess yield of superior land above the yield of the worst land in cultivation or capital employed in the least advantageous circumstances. In Capital, Volume 3, Marx similarly views landed property as a monopoly of the terrestrial globe, but emphasizes that land itself merely creates material use-values (like wheat) and plays no part in creating social value or rent itself, which represents social labor. Both authors attribute rent to the monopoly of differential land qualities, but Marx explicitly clarifies that land creates physical products rather than economic value.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's principle of voluntary federation in Principles and Organization of the International Revolutionary Society compare with John Stuart Mill's view of public spirit in Considerations on Representative Government?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Principles and Organization of the International Revolutionary Society> Every land, every nation, every people, small or large, weak or strong, every region, province, and commune has the absolute right to arrange their own fate, to determine their own existence, to choose their alliances, unite or separate, according to their wishes and needs, without any regard for so-called historic rights and for the political, commercial, or strategic necessities of the states. The unity of the parties in a whole, in order to be true, fruitful, and strong, must be absolutely free. It must only emerge from the local, internal necessities and mutual attractions of the parties—attractions and necessities of which the parties alone will be the judges.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government> He is made to feel himself one of the public, and whatever is their interest to be his interest. Where this school of public spirit does not exist, scarcely any sense is entertained that private persons, in no eminent social situation, owe any duties to society except to obey the laws and submit to the government. There is no unselfish sentiment of identification with the public. Every thought or feeling, either of interest or of duty, is absorbed in the individual and in the family.
reference: In Principles and Organization of the International Revolutionary Society, Bakunin advocates for absolute self-determination and voluntary federation from below, asserting that true unity must emerge freely from local necessities and mutual attraction rather than state compulsion. In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill emphasizes that active participation in local public affairs serves as a school of public spirit that prevents individuals from being absorbed purely in private interests. Both thinkers highlight local self-governance and voluntary association as essential for genuine social cohesion, though Bakunin frames it as an absolute revolutionary right against the state, whereas Mill views local participation as a moral and educational mechanism within representative government.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's assumption about state control of public opinion in On Liberty contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's critique of scientific government in God and the State?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> The time, it is to be hoped, is gone by, when any defence would be necessary of the "liberty of the press" as one of the securities against corrupt or tyrannical government. No argument, we may suppose, can now be needed, against permitting a legislature or an executive, not identified in interest with the people, to prescribe opinions to them, and determine what doctrines or what arguments they shall be allowed to hear. This aspect of the question, besides, has been so often and so triumphantly enforced by preceding writers, that it need not be specially insisted on in this place.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State> Supposing even that it were possible to recognize, amid the conflict of rival ambitions and intrigues, who are the pretenders and who are the real savants, and that a method of election could be found which would not fail to lodge the power in the hands of those whose knowledge is authentic, what guarantee could they offer us of the wisdom and honesty of their government? On the contrary, can we not foresee in these new masters the same follies and the same crimes found in those of former days and of the present time? In the first place, science is not: it is becoming.
reference: In On Liberty, Mill treats it as an established principle that no government or legislature has the legitimate authority to prescribe opinions to the public or dictate what doctrines people may hear. In God and the State, Bakunin extends this distrust of political authority to intellectual elites, arguing that even a government composed of authentic scientific savants would inevitably corrupt its rulers and repeat the crimes of past despots. While Mill focuses on defending individual expression against state-enforced orthodoxy, Bakunin warns that placing political power in the hands of scientific experts converts dynamic knowledge into an oppressive, stationary rule.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's account of the historical origin of gender subjection in The Subjection of Women compare with Mikhail Bakunin's explanation of class privilege in his Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women> In the first place, the opinion in favour of the present system, which entirely subordinates the weaker sex to the stronger, rests upon theory only; for there never has been trial made of any other: so that experience, in the sense in which it is vulgarly opposed to theory, cannot be pretended to have pronounced any verdict. And in the second place, the adoption of this system of inequality never was the result of deliberation, or forethought, or any social ideas, or any notion whatever of what conduced to the benefit of humanity or the good order of society. It arose simply from the fact that from the very earliest twilight of human society, every woman (owing to the value attached to her by men, combined with her inferiority in muscular strength) was found in a state of bondage to some man.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance> But what separates property and capital from labor? What distinguishes the classes economically and politically from one another, what destroys equality and perpetuates inequality, the privilege of the few and the slavery of the many? It is the right of inheritance. Need we demonstrate how the right of inheritance gives rise to every economic, political, and social privilege? Plainly, it alone maintains class differences.
reference: In The Subjection of Women, Mill argues that female subordination originated not from rational deliberation or social utility, but from primitive physical force and bondage from the earliest twilight of human society. In his Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance, Bakunin identifies the right of inheritance as the primary mechanism that petrifies temporary inequalities into traditional class privileges and perpetual slavery. While Mill traces gender inequality to historical coercion converted into legal right, Bakunin identifies the legal right of inheritance as the structural mechanism that maintains economic and political class distinctions across generations.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's economic definition of constant and variable capital in Capital, Volume 1 compare with Mikhail Bakunin's political critique of state equality in The Program of La Démocratie?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume 1> That part of capital then, which is represented by the means of production, by the raw material, auxiliary material and the instruments of labour does not, in the process of production, undergo any quantitative alteration of value. I therefore call it the constant part of capital, or, more shortly, constant capital. On the other hand, that part of capital, represented by labour-power, does, in the process of production, undergo an alteration of value. It both reproduces the equivalent of its own value, and also produces an excess, a surplus-value, which may itself vary, may be more or less according to circumstances. This part of capital is continually being transformed from a constant into a variable magnitude. I therefore call it the variable part of capital, or, shortly, variable capital.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The Program of La Démocratie> Equality without liberty is a noxious fiction created by the rogues to fool the sots. Equality without liberty is the despotism of the State, and the despotic State could not exist a single day without having at least an exploiting and privileged class; the bureaucracy, a hereditary power as in Russia and China, or de facto as in Germany and among you.
reference: In Capital, Volume 1, Marx provides a quantitative economic analysis, defining constant capital as means of production whose value does not alter during production, and variable capital as labor-power, which reproduces its own value and creates surplus-value. In contrast, Bakunin in The Program of La Démocratie presents a political critique of state power, asserting that equality without liberty is a harmful fiction that inevitably produces state despotism and a privileged bureaucratic exploiting class. While Marx locates economic exploitation in the quantitative expansion of variable capital within production, Bakunin focuses on political despotism, arguing that state authority inherently creates a ruling bureaucratic class regardless of professed equality.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's view of the Paris Commune in The Civil War in France contrast with John Stuart Mill's analysis of political disenfranchisement in Considerations on Representative Government?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, The Civil War in France> Imperialism is, at the same time, the most prostitute and the ultimate form of the state power which nascent middle class society had commenced to elaborate as a means of its own emancipation from feudalism, and which full-grown bourgeois society had finally transformed into a means for the enslavement of labor by capital. The direct antithesis to the empire was the Commune. The cry of "social republic," with which the February Revolution was ushered in by the Paris proletariat, did but express a vague aspiration after a republic that was not only to supercede the monarchical form of class rule, but class rule itself. The Commune was the positive form of that republic.

<2-hop: John Stuart Mill, Considerations on Representative Government> Whoever, in an otherwise popular government, has no vote, and no prospect of obtaining it, will either be a permanent malcontent, or will feel as one whom the general affairs of society do not concern; for whom they are to be managed by others; who "has no business with the laws except to obey them," nor with public interests and concerns except as a looker-on.
reference: In The Civil War in France, Marx characterizes the Paris Commune as the direct antithesis to state imperialism and the positive political form meant to supersede not just monarchical government, but class rule itself through working-class self-governance. In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill focuses on electoral participation within representative institutions, arguing that excluding individuals from the vote turns them into malcontents who view laws as imposed by others. While Marx sees proletarian liberation in creating revolutionary communal forms that destroy the bourgeois state engine, Mill seeks to integrate disenfranchised citizens into existing representative government through enfranchisement to foster civic responsibility.

user_input: How does Mikhail Bakunin's concept of revolutionary organization in The Program of the International Brotherhood compare with Marx and Engels' central objective in the Manifesto of the Communist Party?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, The Program of the International Brotherhood> This revolutionary alliance excludes any idea of dictatorship and of a controlling and directive power. It is, however, necessary for the establishment of this revolutionary alliance and for the triumph of the Revolution over reaction that the unity of ideas and of revolutionary action find an organ in the midst of the popular anarchy which will be the life and the energy of the Revolution. This organ should be the secret and universal association of the International Brothers. This association has its origin in the conviction that revolutions are never made by individuals or even by secret societies. They make themselves; they are produced by the force of circumstances, the movement of facts and events.

<2-hop: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party> The distinguishing feature of Communism is not the abolition of property generally, but the abolition of bourgeois property. But modern bourgeois private property is the final and most complete expression of the system of producing and appropriating products, that is based on class antagonisms, on the exploitation of the many by the few. In this sense, the theory of the Communists may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property.
reference: In The Program of the International Brotherhood, Bakunin emphasizes that revolutions arise spontaneously from circumstances rather than being made by individuals, requiring only a secret association of 'International Brothers' to serve as a non-dictatorial organ within popular anarchy. In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels define the core objective of Communism as the explicit abolition of bourgeois private property, which they identify as the ultimate system of class exploitation. While Bakunin focuses on organizing an informal, non-directive vanguard to assist spontaneous popular anarchy, Marx and Engels frame revolutionary purpose around the systematic economic destruction of bourgeois property relations.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's harm principle regarding personal conduct in On Liberty relate to Mikhail Bakunin's proposal for free marriage in the Revolutionary Catechism?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> Acts, of whatever kind, which, without justifiable cause, do harm to others, may be, and in the more important cases absolutely require to be, controlled by the unfavourable sentiments, and, when needful, by the active interference of mankind. The liberty of the individual must be thus far limited; he must not make himself a nuisance to other people. But if he refrains from molesting others in what concerns them, and merely acts according to his own inclination and judgment in things which concern himself, the same reasons which show that opinion should be free, prove also that he should be allowed, without molestation, to carry his opinions into practice at his own cost.

<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Revolutionary Catechism> N. Abolition not of the natural family but of the legal family founded on law and property. reference: In On Liberty, Mill asserts that individual action should be free from societal interference whenever it concerns only the agent and causes no harm to others, limiting restraint solely to preventing harm. In the Revolutionary Catechism, Bakunin applies a similar principle of voluntary choice to personal relationships, demanding the abolition of legal marriage in favor of free unions where consenting adults may unite or separate without state hindrance. Both authors reject external legal compulsion in private personal affairs, with Mill establishing non-harm as the boundary of individual liberty and Bakunin asserting that free choice is the essential condition for moral sincerity in human relationships.

user_input: How does Karl Marx's analysis of self-estrangement in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 compare with Mikhail Bakunin's law of privilege in God and the State?
reference_contexts: <1-hop: Karl Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844> The relation of labor to the act of production within the labor process. reference: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx defines self-estrangement as the process wherein the worker's own labor activity becomes an alien force turned against him, reducing his personal life energy to suffering and powerlessness. In God and the State, Bakunin formulates a psychological law of privilege, asserting that any privileged position—whether political or economic—depraves the mind and heart of the privileged individual. While Marx focuses on how compulsory labor alienates the worker from his own productive activity, Bakunin emphasizes how holding systemic privilege morally and intellectually corrupts the ruling classes.
